intro:
By the end of this track you can follow a payment from your service's `COMMIT` down to the bytes on disk, and back up through the query that reads it. You will know when a write is really durable, how a table becomes 8 KB slotted pages, how the buffer pool decides what stays in memory, why an index is a short, wide B+tree and when an LSM tree fits better, and how the write-ahead log lets a database crash at any moment. Then the read side: which index answers words, time, maps and vectors, how a plan runs and how the planner picks one, why analytics engines store columns, and when a stored, incrementally maintained result beats running the query again. Two case studies, Neo4j and a production PostgreSQL server, put the pieces back together. In practice you can read `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)`, `pg_stats`, `pg_buffercache` and pageinspect output and say what the database is doing and why.

You need to read and write Kotlin and know basic SQL; the SQL track's lessons on joins, aggregation and JDBC come up here, and the Operating systems track's lessons on processes and the page cache come back in lessons 1, 3 and 14. Transactions, MVCC and replication build on this track later, in their own tracks. Install JDK 25 and Docker. The labs compile with release 21, so JDK 21 or newer runs them.

Most labs live in `labs/internals`, packages `sfz.store.l01` to `l12`: you build one piece of a storage engine in plain Kotlin, from a log-structured store, a slotted page, a buffer pool, a B+tree, an LSM store and a write-ahead log to a Volcano executor, a cardinality estimator with a join orderer, a compressed column chunk and an incrementally maintained view. They need no Docker, and their tests are deterministic, crash simulations included. Lessons 8 and 13 model an inverted index, a vector search and Neo4j's record store in `labs/nosql`, also without Docker; lessons 7 and 14 test SQL and server settings against PostgreSQL 18 in `labs/sql`, which needs Docker. Run `./gradlew :internals:test --tests 'sfz.store.l05.*'` from `labs/` for one lesson; the reference answers live in `src/solution`. The Try its run PostgreSQL 18 from `labs/env/postgres.yml`, the other services a lesson names (OpenSearch, TimescaleDB, pgvector, Neo4j), and small demos, one of which runs DuckDB inside the JVM.
cheatsheet:
## The track on one page

| # | Lesson | The problem | The mechanism | Remember |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | A log-structured store | `write` returns before the data is on disk | append-only log, `force` (fsync), a CRC per record, a keydir in RAM, merge | reply OK only after the force; the keydir must fit in RAM and has no order |
| 2 | Pages and heap files | rows of any length in fixed 8 KB pages | slotted page: line pointers at the front, rows at the back; address (page, slot) | DELETE and plain VACUUM don't shrink the file |
| 3 | The buffer pool | a disk read costs far more than a memory read | frames, page table, pins, dirty flags, clock sweep, ring buffers | a pinned page is never evicted; `shared_buffers` near 25% of RAM |
| 4 | B+trees | one row out of millions in a few reads | wide sorted tree of pages, splits, linked leaves; copy-on-write in LMDB | 3 or 4 levels; equality on leading columns, then one range |
| 5 | LSM trees | random inserts dirty whole pages | memtable, immutable SSTables, Bloom filters, compaction | about 10 bits per key for 1% false positives; leveled compaction writes data 10 times or more |
| 6 | Write-ahead logging | pages reach disk long after the commit | log before page, force the log at commit, page LSNs, redo from a checkpoint, full-page images | `synchronous_commit = off` may lose the last commits; `fsync = off` may corrupt |
| 7 | Indexes and EXPLAIN | 14 rows without reading every page | B+tree entries point at heap rows; multicolumn, INCLUDE, partial and expression indexes | read EXPLAIN from the inside out; rows x loops; a cast on the column stops the index |
| 8 | Indexes for text, time and vectors | questions with no single sort order | posting lists in Lucene segments, time chunks and rollups, geohash, R-trees (GiST), H3, HNSW, DiskANN | approximate indexes trade recall; pgvector filters after the HNSW walk |
| 9 | Query execution | running a plan without holding whole results | iterators, nested loop, hash and merge joins, vectorized and compiled engines | batches of about 1,000 values; compiling can cost more than a short query |
| 10 | Query optimization | dozens of plans for three tables | cost model, cardinality estimates, dynamic programming over sets of tables | a bad plan usually means a bad estimate; `CREATE STATISTICS` for correlated columns |
| 11 | Column stores | an analytics scan reads every column | column layout, dictionary, run-length, bit-packing, zone maps, micro-partitions | zone maps skip data only when it is sorted or clustered by the filter column |
| 12 | Materialized views and data cubes | the same expensive aggregate, asked all day | stored results, REFRESH (CONCURRENTLY), delta rules, GROUP BY CUBE | refresh cost follows the data, deltas follow the change; a deleted MIN needs the table |
| 13 | Inside Neo4j | following relationships without index lookups | fixed-size records, doubly linked relationship chains, a page cache, a transaction log | record N sits at byte N x size; page cache = store + indexes + 20% |
| 14 | Running PostgreSQL | one server that survives production | postmaster and a process per connection, shared memory, pg_hba.conf, roles, PgBouncer | the first matching pg_hba line decides; postmaster settings need a restart; pool connections |

## Which structure answers which question

| The question | The structure | Lesson |
|---|---|---|
| this key, this range, this prefix | B+tree | 4, 7 |
| heavy random writes, reads mostly by key | LSM tree | 5 |
| documents with these words, best first | inverted index, BM25 | 8 |
| a time range, rolled up | time chunks, buckets of count, sum, min, max | 8 |
| everything inside this box, nearest to this point | R-tree on GiST, geohash prefix, H3 cell | 8 |
| similar to this embedding | HNSW, IVF, DiskANN, with quantization | 8 |
| a few columns of millions of rows | column store with zone maps | 11 |
| the same aggregate, many times | materialized view, maintained incrementally if it can be | 12 |
| the neighbours of this node | record chains (Neo4j) | 13 |

## Numbers to keep

| What | Value |
|---|---|
| PostgreSQL page | 8 KB; heap row header 24 bytes, line pointer 4 bytes |
| B+tree | hundreds of keys per page, so 3 or 4 levels for any table |
| Bloom filter | 10 bits per key and 7 hash functions: about 1% false positives |
| Checkpoints, PostgreSQL 18 | `checkpoint_timeout` 5 min, `max_wal_size` 1 GB |
| Planner cost units | sequential page 1.0, random page 4.0, row 0.01, operator 0.0025 |
| ANALYZE | 30,000 sampled rows, 100 MCVs and 100 histogram buckets at the default target of 100 |
| Join estimate | rows(R) x rows(S) / max(distinct R.x, distinct S.y) |
| Join Order Benchmark | 52% of PostgreSQL's three-join estimates off by 10x or more |
| BM25 | k1 = 1.2, b = 0.75 |
| pgvector HNSW | `m` 16, `ef_construction` 64, `hnsw.ef_search` 40; iterative scans since 0.8.0 |
| Vectorized batches | X100: about 1,000 values best; DuckDB: 2,048 |
| Zone map granularity | DuckDB row group 122,880 rows; BRIN 128 pages; Snowflake micro-partition 50 to 500 MB; Redshift block 1 MB |
| Hash table memory | `work_mem` (4 MB) x `hash_mem_multiplier` (2) |
| Neo4j records | node 15 bytes, relationship 34, property 41 |
| A PostgreSQL connection | one process; about 1.5 MB of private memory when idle; `max_connections` 100 by default |

## Easy to confuse

| | One | The other |
|---|---|---|
| B+tree vs LSM tree | updates pages in place; a read follows one path down; a random insert dirties a whole page | appends to a memtable and writes sorted files; writes are sequential; a read may check several files, and compaction rewrites data |
| Buffer pool vs OS page cache | the database's own cache: it knows pins, dirty pages and the WAL rule | the kernel's cache of file data; PostgreSQL reads through it too, so a page can be cached twice |
| Exact vs approximate index | B+tree, GiST: every match, always | HNSW, IVF: fast, but recall below 1.0 and filters applied after the walk |
| Nested loop vs hash join | outer x inner work, or one index lookup per outer row; any condition; best for few outer rows | outer + inner work; equality only; needs memory for the build side |
| Vectorized vs compiled | prebuilt operators over batches; better at hiding memory stalls; no compile time | one generated loop per pipeline; fewer instructions; pays to compile each query |
| Zone map (BRIN) vs B+tree | min and max per block range: tiny, helps only columns that follow the row order | an entry per row: precise in any order, much bigger |
| Index vs materialized view | a copy of rows in another order | a copy of a computed result; stale until refreshed or maintained |
| REFRESH vs REFRESH CONCURRENTLY | ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock, readers wait; usually less work | needs a unique index; readers keep reading; reruns the query and then diffs |

## Looking inside PostgreSQL

| To see | Use |
|---|---|
| the rows and line pointers of a page | `SELECT * FROM heap_page_items(get_raw_page('t', 0))` (pageinspect) |
| what is cached | `pg_buffercache`, and `Buffers: shared hit / read` in `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` |
| an index's pages | `bt_metap`, `bt_page_items` (pageinspect) |
| the WAL | `pg_current_wal_lsn()`, `pg_waldump` |
| what a plan did | `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE)`: estimated `rows=` against `actual rows=`, times `loops` |
| what the planner knows | `pg_stats`, `pg_stats_ext`; fix correlated columns with `CREATE STATISTICS` |
| what JIT compiled | the `JIT:` section of `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE)` (shown only with costs) |
| who holds a lock on a view | `pg_locks` filtered on `relation = 'name'::regclass` |
| how a setting changes | `pg_settings.context`, then `pending_restart` after `SELECT pg_reload_conf()` |

## When something goes wrong, ask first

- Data lost after a crash: was the OK sent before a force, or with `synchronous_commit = off`?
- Query got slow: in EXPLAIN ANALYZE, which is the lowest node whose estimated and actual rows differ by 10x or more?
- A vector search returns too few rows: is a WHERE clause filtering after the index walk?
- A dashboard freezes every few minutes: is a plain REFRESH holding an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock on its view?
- Analytics hurts the primary: can the scan move to a column store, loaded in batches and sorted by the filter column?
- Pods fail with `remaining connection slots are reserved`: do the pools add up to more than `max_connections`?
recap: A write is durable only after `force` (fsync) returns. Logs make that affordable: append sequentially, force once per batch, and check a CRC per record after a crash.
Tables are files of 8 KB slotted pages, and a row's address is (page, slot). The buffer pool caches pages with pins, dirty flags and a clock sweep, on top of the OS page cache.

A B+tree reads one page per level and updates pages in place. An LSM tree turns random writes into sequential files and pays with compaction and multi-file reads; no design wins on reads, writes and space at once.
The write-ahead log is forced at commit and always reaches disk before the pages it describes. Recovery replays it from the last checkpoint, and page LSNs make replay safe to repeat.

Each index is a copy organised for one shape of question: B+trees for one sort order; posting lists, time chunks, R-trees, geohashes and H3 cells, and HNSW or DiskANN graphs for the rest. Every one costs writes, and the approximate ones cost recall.

A plan is a tree of iterators; nested loops cost outer x inner (or a lookup per outer row), hash joins outer + inner. Vectorized and compiled engines remove the per-row overhead and end up close; compiling has its own cost.
The planner picks the cheapest plan for its estimates, and estimates are where it fails: correlated columns and joins multiply the errors. Fix the lowest misestimate before forcing a plan.

Column stores keep each column together, compress it, and skip chunks with zone maps; cloud warehouses prune micro-partitions and blocks the same way, so sorting and clustering decide what a query reads.

A materialized view trades write work for cheap reads. A refresh recomputes everything; incremental maintenance applies deltas, which are easy for count and sum and hard for MIN under deletes, joins and big batches. A data cube stores every grouping of its dimensions.

Real databases are these parts put together: Neo4j is fixed-size records behind a page cache and a transaction log, and a PostgreSQL server is a process per connection around shared buffers and a WAL, guarded by pg_hba.conf and roles.

quiz.q: A ledger service writes each entry with `FileChannel.write` and replies OK at once. The machine loses power a millisecond later. What may have happened to the entry?
options: Nothing: `write` returned, so the bytes are on disk
It may be lost: `write` only copied it into the kernel's page cache, and only `force` waits for the drive
It is half-written, and the next start fails
It is safe if the file was opened in append mode
quiz.why: `write` returns once the kernel has the bytes in memory. They reach the drive later, unless `force` (fsync) is called and returns first. A torn last record is possible too, which is why logs carry a CRC per record, but the main point is that the OK went out before the data was durable.

quiz.q: `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` shows `Buffers: shared read=8000` for a query that finished in 30 ms, and the disks show no reads at all. How?
options: EXPLAIN counts reads it planned, not reads it did
The pages were in the buffer pool after all; `read` is a rounding error
`read` means the pages weren't in `shared_buffers`; PostgreSQL asked the kernel, which had them in the OS page cache
The query ran on a replica
quiz.why: PostgreSQL's buffer pool sits on top of the kernel's page cache, and it reads files through it. A miss in `shared_buffers` is counted as `read` even when the kernel serves the page from memory in microseconds. That double caching is why `shared_buffers` starts near 25% of RAM rather than most of it.

quiz.q: A fraud service inserts 50,000 events a second keyed by random UUIDs and reads them back by key, rarely by range. Why might an LSM tree suit it better than a B+tree, and what does it pay?
options: The LSM tree writes sorted files sequentially instead of dirtying a random page per insert; it pays with compaction rewrites and reads that may check several files
The B+tree appends random UUIDs at the end of its last leaf, so it wins on writes too
The LSM tree wins on writes and on reads, with no cost
The B+tree is better, because Bloom filters make its range scans fast
quiz.why: Random keys land on random leaf pages, so a B+tree dirties (and logs) a whole 8 KB page for a small insert. An LSM tree buffers writes in a memtable and flushes them as one sorted file, then merges files in the background: write amplification from compaction, and point reads that may look in several files, which Bloom filters make cheaper. Only ascending keys fill a B+tree's last leaf; Bloom filters belong to LSM trees and don't help range scans.

quiz.q: A payments service commits a transfer and gets OK. A second later the server loses power. The changed table pages were still dirty in the buffer pool. What does PostgreSQL find at restart?
options: The transfer is lost, because its pages never reached the data files
The data files are corrupt, and a backup must be restored
Half of the transfer, because pages are written one at a time
The transfer, because its WAL records were forced at commit; recovery replays them onto the old pages from the last checkpoint
quiz.why: The commit rule says COMMIT returns only once the log is durable past the commit record; the pages can be written any time later. Recovery starts at the last checkpoint's redo point and reapplies every record whose LSN is newer than the page's, so the transfer reappears whole. Corruption is what `fsync = off` risks, not a normal power cut, and a torn page is restored from the full-page image in the WAL.

quiz.q: A fraud screen runs `SELECT ... FROM disputes WHERE merchant_id = ? ORDER BY embedding <-> ? LIMIT 10` on a pgvector HNSW index with default settings. For small merchants it often shows 0 to 3 similar disputes, though they have dozens. What is going on?
options: The HNSW index is corrupt and needs a REINDEX
The index walk collects about 40 candidates and the WHERE clause runs afterwards, so a selective filter leaves few rows; iterative scans or a different index for the filter fix it
LIMIT 10 is applied before the distance is computed
HNSW can't index vectors from more than one merchant
quiz.why: pgvector applies filters after the approximate scan: with `hnsw.ef_search` 40 the walk returns 40 candidates by distance, and only the ones for that merchant survive. `SET hnsw.iterative_scan = relaxed_order` keeps walking until enough rows pass; a partial index or exact search on the merchant's few rows also works. Nothing is broken, which is why the bug goes unnoticed.

quiz.q: A screen shows the 10 newest payments with their merchant names; `merchants.id` has a primary-key index. A nightly report joins all 2 million payments with 10,000 merchants. Which join suits each?
options: Hash join for both
Nested loop for both
Index nested loop for the screen (10 index lookups), hash join for the report (each table read once)
Merge join for both, because the primary key is sorted
quiz.why: With 10 outer rows, one index lookup per row touches a handful of pages; building a hash table of 10,000 merchants first would cost more. For 2 million rows, a nested loop would do 2 million lookups or 20 billion comparisons, while a hash join builds a table of the merchants once and probes it per payment.

quiz.q: Which statement about PostgreSQL's planner is true?
options: It picks the cheapest plan for its row estimates, which come from sampled per-column statistics and assume conditions on different columns are independent
It always finds the fastest plan, given an index
It runs the candidate plans on a sample and keeps the fastest
It learns correlations between columns from multicolumn indexes
quiz.why: The planner prices plans with a cost model fed by cardinality estimates, then searches join orders by dynamic programming. The search is exact for its inputs, so when the plan is bad it is usually because an estimate is far off, often from correlated columns. Only `CREATE STATISTICS` gives it cross-column statistics; indexes don't.

quiz.q: Settlement records from 40 acquirers are written to Parquet in arrival order. A reconciliation query filters on `acquirer_id = 17` and one settlement day, and the reader still reads every row group. What lets it skip most of them?
options: Bigger row groups, so there are fewer to read
zstd compression on top of the encodings
A B+tree index stored next to the file
Sorting each file by acquirer and settlement day before writing it, so each row group's min and max cover a narrow range
quiz.why: Readers skip a row group when its column statistics, the min and max, rule out the condition. In arrival order every row group holds most acquirers and days, so nothing can be ruled out. Sorted data gives each row group a narrow range that most queries miss. Compression and bigger groups make reads cheaper but don't skip anything.

quiz.q: A materialized view of per-merchant daily totals over a 200-million-row ledger takes 6 minutes to refresh. The business wants it within a minute of every payment. What fits?
options: Incremental maintenance: apply each payment as a delta (count + 1, sum + amount), with pg_ivm or a streaming view, so the work follows the change rather than the ledger
REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW every 30 seconds
REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY every 30 seconds, since it only applies the differences
Drop the view and run the aggregate on every page load
quiz.why: A refresh, plain or concurrent, reruns the whole query, so it can't finish in 30 seconds when it needs 6 minutes; CONCURRENTLY only applies the differences after recomputing everything. Count and sum have simple delta rules, so maintaining them per payment costs one view row each. Running the aggregate on every load moves the 6 minutes onto the readers.

quiz.q: Thirty pods each run a connection pool of 10 against a PostgreSQL server with `max_connections = 100` and 8 cores. New pods fail to connect. Which change addresses the cause?
options: Raise `max_connections` to 400 so every pod fits
Put PgBouncer in transaction pooling mode in front, so 300 client connections share a few dozen server processes, after checking the service keeps no session state
Give the service's role SUPERUSER so it can use the reserved slots
Lower `work_mem` so each connection uses less memory
quiz.why: Every PostgreSQL connection is a process forked by the postmaster. 300 processes on 8 cores fight for the CPU even when the cap allows them, so raising it trades an error for a slower server. A pooler lets many client connections share a few busy server connections, one transaction at a time; it breaks only session state such as `SET` without LOCAL, LISTEN and advisory locks. A superuser application is a security mistake, and work_mem doesn't change the count.
